title: Quiz: Splines, Cross-Validation, and Missing Values

questions.text: What is the key difference between a natural spline ns(x, df) and a polynomial poly(x, df)?
options: Natural splines use fewer knots than polynomials
Natural splines are linear in the tails, preventing extreme extrapolation outside the training range; polynomials can oscillate wildly outside the data
Polynomials are always smoother than natural splines
Natural splines require more data points than polynomials
questions.explanation: Natural splines impose a linearity constraint in the tails (beyond the outermost knots). This prevents the extreme oscillation that high-degree polynomials exhibit when extrapolating beyond the training data. Inside the data range, both can be equally flexible for the same df.

questions.text: In 10-fold cross-validation, you train on all 10 folds and test on each fold in turn.
questions.explanation: In K-fold CV, you train on K−1 folds and test on the remaining 1 fold. For 10-fold CV: train on 9 folds, test on the 10th, repeat 10 times (each fold serves as the test set once). The CV estimate is the mean test error across all 10 rounds.

questions.text: You run 10-fold CV for df = 1 to 8 on a dataset. The CV-RMSE curve decreases from df=1 to df=4 then increases. What is the optimal df?
options: df = 1, because simpler models generalise better
df = 8, because training RMSE is lowest
df = 4, because it minimises the CV-RMSE (out-of-sample error)
df = 6, because the one-SE rule adds 2 to the minimum
questions.explanation: The minimum CV-RMSE is at df = 4. This is the optimal choice — it balances bias (underfitting for df < 4) and variance (overfitting for df > 4). The one-SE rule would choose the smallest df whose CV-RMSE is within one standard error of the minimum at df = 4 — which might be df = 3, not df = 6.

questions.text: What is the practical advantage of na.action = na.exclude over the default na.omit in lm()?
options: na.exclude fits the model on more data points
na.exclude preserves NA positions in residuals and predictions, making it easy to align output with the original data frame
na.exclude imputes missing values before fitting
na.exclude treats NA as zero in the response
questions.explanation: With na.exclude, the residuals and predictions vectors have the same length as the original data frame, with NA at positions where data was missing. This makes it straightforward to merge model output back into the original data. With na.omit (the default), the output is shorter, causing index misalignment.

questions.text: In multiple imputation with m = 5, Rubin's pooling rule combines 5 sets of coefficient estimates. What does the 'between-imputation variance' capture?
options: The variance due to random sampling of the training data
The additional uncertainty due to not knowing the true values of the missing data
The variance of the response variable across imputed datasets
The standard deviation of the five imputed datasets
questions.explanation: Between-imputation variance measures how much the coefficient estimates vary across the m imputed datasets. Large variation means the missing data are informative — there is substantial uncertainty about what the true values are. Rubin's rules add this between-imputation component to the within-imputation variance to get the total standard error.

questions.text: Standard errors from multiple imputation are always at least as large as those from complete-case analysis (listwise deletion), because MI accounts for additional uncertainty due to missing values.
questions.explanation: MI inflates standard errors by adding the between-imputation variance component. Complete-case analysis ignores the uncertainty due to missingness, so its standard errors are too small (overconfident). MI provides the statistically valid estimate of precision under missing data.
